newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wage agreements not yet moderating - HSBC.
newsitem.headline: Australian wage agreements not yet moderating - HSBC.

text.p: The pace of Australian wages growth, as measured by federal enterprise bargaining agreements (EBA), is showing no signs of moderating from the pace of the December quarter, a study by HSBC markets has shown.

The first HSBC Markets wages report, prepared by former Department of Industrial Relations economist Grant Fitzner, said that March quarter enterprise barging agreements could pay an average annualised wage increase of a little under five percent, compared to 4.4 percent in the December quarter.
However, while EBAs were not showing signs of a slowdown, other signs were pointing to moderate wage growth through 1997.
"This could result in a March quarter AAWI as reported by DIR of a little under five percent per employee," he said.
While enterprise agreements were not showing any sign of moderation, economic and industrial factors were holding back wage pressures, and business surveys pointed to wage moderation.
The living wage claim decision last week, granting a A$10 a week safety net adjustment and reintroducing a federal minimum wage, was seen having a modest impact on wages growth.
The pressures working to hold back wages included a sluggish labour market, falling mortgage rates and inflation, and a tougher industrial relations climate for unions, Fitzner said.
Surveys were showing moderation in the wage rises employers expected to pay, as well as a strong wage-productivity link.
However, overall wage agreements were only slowly responding to the low inflation enviroment, HSBC said.

"An important message for financial markets from the review of first quarter agreements is that outcomes are only slowly responding to low inflation, and that the current rate of increase is consistent with low inflation and an unchanged monetary policy stance only so long as the award stream sees marginal growth," HSBC chief economist John Edwards said.
